analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels to show all mandatory fees in their advertised room rates.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Hotels and motels often advertise a low room rate and then add mandatory charges — resort fees, facility fees — that a guest must pay but never sees in the advertised price. This bill would require those fees to be included in the advertised rate, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing the rule as an unfair or deceptive practice. It also exempts government taxes from the all-in price. The bill was introduced by one member with no cosponsors and never advanced out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers booking hotel rooms, who would see the true price of a stay upfront instead of discovering mandatory resort or facility fees at checkout. Budget travelers comparison-shopping on price benefit most, since hidden fees make advertised rates misleading.

how_it_helps.text: Requires lodging operators to include every mandatory fee or charge in any advertised rental rate [S3].
Exempts only government-assessed taxes and fees from the all-in advertised price [S3].
Enforces the rule through the Federal Trade Commission as an unfair or deceptive practice, carrying the penalties of the FTC Act [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The lodging industry, which would have to stop quoting rates without mandatory resort and facility fees, and could lose bookings if all-in prices look higher than competitors' advertised rates. Enforcement costs fall on the FTC.

drawbacks.text: The exemption for government-assessed taxes and fees means advertised prices still would not include sales and occupancy taxes, so the displayed price still falls short of the final bill [S3].
The bill relies entirely on FTC enforcement, which is case-by-case; it does not create a private right of action for individual guests who were misled [S3].
A good-faith objection from the industry is that all-in pricing makes its rates look higher than competitors quoting base rates, an advertising disadvantage even for hotels that charge no fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but narrow: clearer advertised prices for hotel stays, ending the practice of mandatory fees surfacing at checkout. The cost to hotels is also real but modest — honest pricing rather than lower total prices, since the fees themselves remain legal. A reasonable bill, though the tax exemption keeps advertised prices slightly below the true final cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee, and died there when the 117th Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gosar introduced the bill on March 15, 2022 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce [S5].
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The hotel industry kept the ability to advertise stripped-down room rates with mandatory resort and facility fees added later, and consumers kept paying the same fees without seeing them in the quoted price.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The lodging industry and hidden-fee pricing

for.name: Rep. Paul Gosar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill; it sat in committee and its consumer protection subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote, which it would have needed to become law.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a cosponsor from either party, so the record shows no partisan split on the merits; its sole sponsor was a Republican and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: Mandatory resort and facility fees let lodging operators advertise low room rates and collect more at checkout; the bill would force those fees into the advertised price. Guests pay the same fees either way, but all-in pricing removes the advertising advantage that hidden fees create.

Platform fees are charged as a condition of booking, so a broad reading of the bill could reach booking sites and change how they display prices. Consumers get clearer price comparisons; platforms lose the ability to quote lower headline prices.
